Name: AS-REP Roasting
Description:
# Description

One or more Active Directory accounts have Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication (UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH) set. Without pre-authentication, any unauthenticated party on the network can request an AS-REP for the account and receive material encrypted with the account's password-derived key — a hash crackable offline at GPU speed (hashcat mode 18200), with no interaction with the account and no lockout risk to the attacker.

# Impact

Offline recovery of the account's cleartext password with no account lockout and minimal logging on the target — the request itself generates a single Kerberos AS-REQ, not a logon attempt. A recovered password yields authenticated domain access as the affected principal; escalation potential depends on the account's privileges and group memberships (service accounts and legacy admin accounts are frequent hits for this flag).

# Replication Steps
  • Enumerate accounts with the flag set and request their AS-REPs unauthenticated: GetNPUsers.py {{DOMAIN}}/ -no-pass -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip {{TARGET_HOST}} -format hashcat
  • Crack offline: hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hashes wordlist.txt

Accounts confirmed vulnerable to AS-REP roasting: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Remove the flag from every affected account: Get-ADUser -Filter 'DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true' | Set-ADAccountControl -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false. Enforce a strong, unique password policy on the accounts above and migrate service identities to (group) Managed Service Accounts, which rotate a 120-character password automatically and are not roastable in the same way. Alert on Kerberos AS-REQ traffic with pre-authentication type 0 (Event ID 4768, PreAuthType absent) as a detection control.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1558.004 — Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting
  • CWE-522 — Insufficiently Protected Credentials
  • Microsoft: Kerberos pre-authentication

Name: Kerberoasting
Description:
# Description

One or more accounts have a Service Principal Name (SPN) registered in Active Directory. Any authenticated domain user — no elevated rights required — can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for these SPNs; the ticket is encrypted with the service account's password-derived key and can be cracked offline (hashcat mode 13100) to recover the cleartext service password. The request itself is legitimate Kerberos traffic that generates no failed-logon signal on the target.

# Impact

Recovery of service-account passwords — frequently high-privilege identities (SQL, Exchange, SCCM, backup agents) provisioned years earlier with a weak or static password — leading to lateral movement and privilege escalation. Cracking is entirely offline and undetectable on the target; only the initial TGS request is observable.

# Replication Steps
  • Request TGS tickets for every SPN-registered account: GetUserSPNs.py {{DOMAIN}}/user:pass -dc-ip {{TARGET_HOST}} -request -outputfile kerb.hashes
  • Crack offline: hashcat -m 13100 kerb.hashes wordlist.txt

Service accounts confirmed vulnerable to Kerberoasting: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Move every SPN-bearing account identified above to a Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) with a 120-character, automatically rotated password. Where an SPN on a standard user account is unavoidable, enforce a 25+ character random password and AES-only ticket encryption (disable RC4 for the account) so the ticket is not crackable at reasonable cost. Alert on abnormal TGS request volume per user (Event ID 4769) as a detection control — a single account requesting many distinct service tickets in a short window is a strong roasting indicator.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1558.003 — Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
  • CWE-522 — Insufficiently Protected Credentials
  • Microsoft: Group Managed Service Accounts overview

Name: AD CS - Vulnerable Certificate Template or CA (ESC)
Description:
# Description

Active Directory Certificate Services exposes one or more misconfigurations in the ESC1–ESC17 classes that permit certificate-based privilege escalation. Depending on the class, a low-privileged principal can enroll for a certificate that authenticates as a higher-privileged principal — including a Domain Controller (ESC8 via HTTP web enrollment + NTLM relay, or ESC1's enrollee-supplied SAN) — without ever touching a credential belonging to that principal.

# Impact

Certificate-based authentication as a higher-privileged principal, frequently escalating directly to Domain Admin / Domain Controller compromise. Unlike a stolen password, a certificate foothold is persistent: it remains valid until expiry and survives a password reset on the impersonated account, making it a durable, hard-to-detect re-entry point.

# Replication Steps
  • Enumerate vulnerable templates/CAs: certipy find -u user@{{DOMAIN}} -p pass -dc-ip {{TARGET_HOST}} -vulnerable -stdout
  • Abuse per class, e.g. ESC1: certipy req -u user@{{DOMAIN}} -template <tmpl> -upn administrator@{{DOMAIN}}

Vulnerable template(s)/CA(s) identified: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Remediate per class: remove enrollee-supplied-SAN (CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT) from the template(s) above, require manager approval on sensitive templates, and restrict template enrollment/write rights to the principals that genuinely need them. Disable HTTP Web Enrollment or enforce Extended Protection for Authentication plus channel binding on it, and enable strong certificate mapping (KB5014754) so an issued certificate cannot silently impersonate an account via a weak UPN/SAN match.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1649 — Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
  • SpecterOps: Certified Pre-Owned (ESC1–ESC8)
  • Microsoft KB5014754 — Certificate-based authentication changes

Name: DCSync - Domain Credential Database Extraction
Description:
# Description

An account with directory-replication rights performed a DCSync (DRSUAPI replication) against a domain controller and extracted NTLM hashes from the NTDS.dit database — the entire credential store of the domain. Possessing (and exercising) Replicating Directory Changes / Replicating Directory Changes All rights is Domain-Admin-equivalent regardless of the account's nominal group membership.

# Impact

Total domain compromise. Every account's password hash is available for pass-the-hash and offline cracking, and — via the krbtgt account's hash specifically — Golden-Ticket forgery grants indefinite, unrestricted domain persistence that survives ordinary password rotations.

# Replication Steps
  • Replicate the credential database remotely: secretsdump.py {{DOMAIN}}/da:pass@{{TARGET_HOST}} -just-dc

Scope of extraction: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Treat the entire domain as compromised: rotate all credentials, reset the krbtgt password twice (with AD replication completing between resets), and rebuild trust from a known-good state rather than assuming a single account cleanup is sufficient. Restrict Replicating Directory Changes/...All rights to Domain Controllers only (audit for any user/service account holding them), and alert on DRSUAPI replication requests sourced from a non-DC host (Event ID 4662 with the replication GUIDs, correlated to source IP).

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1003.006 — OS Credential Dumping: DCSync
  • CWE-522 — Insufficiently Protected Credentials
  • Microsoft: Reset the krbtgt account password

Name: SMB Signing Not Required
Description:
# Description

The host(s) at {{AFFECTED}} do not require SMB message signing. An attacker positioned on the network — including via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning, a rogue DHCP/DNS answer, or any coercion primitive (PetitPotam/PrinterBug-class) — can relay a captured or coerced authentication attempt to these hosts (NTLM relay) and act as the coerced user without ever recovering their password.

# Impact

Authentication relay leading to authenticated file-share access, remote command execution via SMB (PsExec-style), or local administrator access on the relay target — and, when the relayed identity is itself privileged or the target is a Domain Controller, a direct path to domain compromise. This is a common last link in a poisoning-to-domain-admin chain, not an isolated weakness.

# Replication Steps
  • Confirm signing is not required: nxc smb {{TARGET_HOST}} — observe signing:False
  • Relay a captured/coerced authentication: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support
Recommendation:
Enforce SMB signing on all hosts via Group Policy (Microsoft network server/client: Digitally sign communications (always)), and require it unconditionally on Domain Controllers where it is enabled by default in current baselines but still worth confirming. Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS (see the companion poisoning finding) to remove the most common coercion primitive feeding this relay path, since signing alone does not stop credential capture — only the relay leg.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1557.001 — LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay
  • CWE-300 — Channel Accessible by Non-Endpoint (Man-in-the-Middle)
  • Microsoft: Overview of Server Message Block signing

Name: SMB Null Session Allowed
Description:
# Description

The host(s) at {{AFFECTED}} permit anonymous (null) SMB sessions — an unauthenticated connection with the empty username/password (-u '' -p '') is accepted for RPC-based enumeration, allowing unauthenticated discovery of local/domain users, groups, shares, and password policy without a single valid credential.

# Impact

Unauthenticated reconnaissance that directly seeds later attacks: enumerated usernames feed targeted password-spray and AS-REP/Kerberoast candidate lists, enumerated shares reveal additional attack surface, and the password policy (lockout threshold, complexity) tells an attacker exactly how aggressively they can spray without tripping a lockout.

# Replication Steps
  • Enumerate over the null session: enum4linux-ng -A {{TARGET_HOST}}
  • Confirm and pull users/shares directly: nxc smb {{TARGET_HOST}} -u '' -p '' --shares --users
Recommendation:
Restrict anonymous access: set RestrictAnonymous = 2 and RestrictAnonymousSAM = 1 (or the equivalent Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares Group Policy setting) domain-wide. Remove shares that have no business justification and tighten ACLs on the ones that remain, so a null session — even if later re-enabled by accident — discloses nothing exploitable.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1135 — Network Share Discovery
  • CWE-287 — Improper Authentication
  • CIS Microsoft Windows Benchmarks — anonymous access controls

Name: SMBv1 Enabled
Description:
# Description

The legacy SMBv1 dialect is enabled and negotiable on {{AFFECTED}}. SMBv1 is a deprecated, unauthenticated-by-design-weakness protocol carrying a documented history of critical, wormable remote-code-execution vulnerabilities — most notably the EternalBlue class (MS17-010, CVE-2017-0144) weaponized by WannaCry and NotPetya.

# Impact

Unauthenticated remote code execution as SYSTEM on the affected host if it is unpatched for the MS17-010 class, and — because the exploit requires no credentials and propagates over SMB — rapid, wormable lateral spread across any other SMBv1-reachable host on the network.

# Replication Steps
  • Confirm the dialect is offered: nxc smb {{TARGET_HOST}} — observe SMB1 in the supported dialects, or nmap --script smb-protocols -p445 {{TARGET_HOST}}
Recommendation:
Disable SMBv1 everywhere it is not explicitly required by legacy hardware/software (Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol, or the equivalent GPO), and confirm hosts are fully patched for MS17-010 and subsequent SMB CVEs regardless. Where a legacy dependency genuinely requires SMBv1, isolate that host on its own segment with no route to the rest of the environment.

References

  • Microsoft MS17-010 / CVE-2017-0144 — SMBv1 remote code execution
  • CWE-327 — Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
  • Microsoft: Stop using SMB1

Name: LLMNR / NBT-NS / mDNS Poisoning
Description:
# Description

Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR), NBT-NS, and/or mDNS are enabled on the local broadcast network segment. When a host fails ordinary DNS resolution (a typo'd share name, a stale mapped drive, a misconfigured print/proxy lookup) it falls back to a broadcast query; an attacker on the same broadcast domain answers first and coerces the victim into authenticating to it, capturing its NetNTLMv2 challenge/response.

# Impact

Capture of NetNTLMv2 hashes for offline cracking, or immediate relay (see the companion "SMB Signing Not Required" finding) to a signing-not-required host for interactive access with no cracking at all — a classic, low-effort path from a passive network foothold straight to credentials or code execution.

# Replication Steps
  • Passively capture: responder -I eth0 -wf — hashes arrive as victims resolve unresolvable names
  • Relay instead of cracking: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support

Credentials captured: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Disable LLMNR via Group Policy (Turn off multicast name resolution), disable NBT-NS (per-adapter, or the DHCP option pushed fleet-wide), and disable mDNS where it serves no purpose. Enforce SMB and LDAP signing so a captured hash cannot simply be relayed even if poisoning is not fully eliminated, and ensure DNS is correctly and completely configured so resolution never needs the broadcast fallback in the first place.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1557.001 — LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and Relay
  • CWE-300 — Channel Accessible by Non-Endpoint (Man-in-the-Middle)

Name: Weak or Guessable Credentials
Description:
# Description

Authenticated credential testing (targeted brute-force / password-spray) against network service(s) in scope confirmed one or more accounts accept a weak, default, or otherwise guessable password.

# Impact

Direct authenticated access as the affected account, enabling lateral movement and further privilege escalation proportional to that account's rights and group memberships. A single weak credential is frequently the initial foothold an otherwise well-hardened environment lacks.

# Replication Steps
  • Credential testing against the identified service(s) confirmed the account(s) below authenticate successfully with the tested password: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Reset every affected credential to a strong, unique value; enforce a robust password policy (length over complexity, breached-password screening) and require MFA wherever the service supports it. Remove or rotate default/service-installer accounts rather than leaving them at their shipped password. Monitor for password-spray patterns — many failed logons (4625) across many distinct accounts from one source in a short window, rather than many attempts against one account.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1110 — Brute Force
  • CWE-521 — Weak Password Requirements
  • NIST SP 800-63B — Digital Identity Guidelines

Name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
Description:
# Description

The application at {{TARGET_URL}} reflects or stores attacker-controlled input into a page without adequate output encoding for the context it lands in (HTML body, attribute, or script), allowing execution of arbitrary JavaScript in a victim's browser under the site's own origin.

# Impact

Session hijacking, credential theft via a fake login overlay, forced state-changing actions on behalf of the victim, and phishing/defacement. A stored instance is materially worse than a reflected one: it fires for every user who later views the injected content, with no link for the victim to click.

# Replication Steps
  • Inject a probe such as <script>alert(document.domain)</script> (or a context-appropriate payload, e.g. an attribute-breakout or event-handler payload where angle brackets are filtered) into the identified parameter and observe execution.

Location(s): {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Apply context-aware output encoding to all untrusted data (HTML-entity encode for body context, JS-string encode inside <script>, attribute encode inside a tag attribute) and prefer a framework's auto-escaping templates over raw HTML sinks (innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html). Deploy a strict Content-Security-Policy as defense-in-depth, and set HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite on session cookies so a successful injection still cannot read the session token directly.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A03:2021 — Injection
  • OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • CWE-79 — Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

Name: SQL Injection
Description:
# Description

A parameter at {{TARGET_URL}} is concatenated directly into a SQL query rather than bound as a parameter, allowing an attacker to alter the query's logic — add conditions, union in additional result sets, or chain statements — via crafted input.

# Impact

Unauthorized read or modification of database contents (potentially the full contents of every table the application's DB account can reach), authentication bypass, and — depending on the database engine, its configured privileges, and any file-system or command-execution features left enabled — a path to remote code execution or lateral movement to the database host itself.

# Replication Steps
  • Confirm with a boolean- or time-based probe (e.g. ' AND 1=1-- vs ' AND 1=2--, or ' OR SLEEP(5)--), then enumerate: sqlmap -u '{{TARGET_URL}}' --batch

Location(s): {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Use parameterized queries / prepared statements (or a vetted ORM that does so by default) for every query touching user input — string concatenation into SQL must not appear anywhere in the codebase. Run the application's database account under least privilege (no FILE/xp_cmdshell-class rights, no access beyond the schemas it needs), validate and allow-list input as defense-in-depth, and treat a WAF rule as a stopgap, never the fix.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A03:2021 — Injection
  • OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • CWE-89 — Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command

Name: Exposed Version Control Directory (.git)
Description:
# Description

A version-control directory (.git/) is served at {{TARGET_URL}}, exposing the repository's full object database and commit history to any anonymous requester — equivalent to handing out read access to the source repository itself.

# Impact

Full reconstruction of the application's source code and its entire commit history, frequently surfacing hard-coded credentials/API keys that were later removed (but remain in history), internal endpoint names, and logic an attacker can now review offline for further vulnerabilities at their own pace.

# Replication Steps
  • Confirm exposure: request {{TARGET_URL}}/.git/HEAD and check for a valid ref response.
  • Reconstruct the repository: git-dumper {{TARGET_URL}}/.git/ ./dump

Location(s): {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Block access to VCS metadata directories at the web server / reverse proxy (a deny rule for /.git/ and any other dotfile directory), and prefer deploying from a build artifact that never includes .git in the first place rather than relying on an access rule alone. Rotate any secret that appears anywhere in the exposed history, not just the current tip — a credential removed in a later commit is still fully readable in an earlier one.

References

  • CWE-527 — Exposure of Version-Control Repository to an Unauthorized Control Sphere
  • OWASP Top 10 A05:2021 — Security Misconfiguration

Name: Sensitive Information Disclosure
Description:
# Description

The application at {{TARGET_URL}} discloses sensitive information to unauthenticated users — verbose stack traces, internal file paths, software version banners, or a status/metrics endpoint (such as Apache server-status or an unauthenticated /metrics) — that should not be reachable without authentication.

# Impact

Provides an attacker reconnaissance that accelerates targeted exploitation (exact software versions narrow the CVE search immediately), and disclosed internals occasionally include credentials, session tokens, or internal hostnames that are directly actionable rather than merely informative.

# Replication Steps
  • Retrieve the disclosing endpoint(s) directly and review the response body for internals: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Disable verbose/debug error output in production so a failure returns a generic message, not a stack trace; restrict or remove status/metrics/diagnostic endpoints, or bind them to localhost and require authentication if they must remain reachable. Suppress version banners on public-facing services, and review response bodies during code review for unintentional data exposure rather than relying solely on a scanner to catch it.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A05:2021 — Security Misconfiguration
  • CWE-200 — Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

Name: Missing or Weak HTTP Security Headers
Description:
# Description

Responses from {{TARGET_URL}} omit, or weakly configure, defense-in-depth headers such as Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, and a frame-ancestors policy / X-Frame-Options.

# Impact

Low risk in isolation, but increases the exploitability and blast radius of other issues on the same origin: a missing CSP removes a backstop against XSS, a missing HSTS header leaves a window for protocol downgrade on the first visit, and a missing frame-ancestors policy permits clickjacking. Meaningful primarily as defense-in-depth alongside the fixes for any other findings on this target.

# Replication Steps
  • Inspect response headers: curl -I {{TARGET_URL}}
Recommendation:
Add a strict Content-Security-Policy tailored to the application's actual script/style sources (not a blanket unsafe-inline), Strict-Transport-Security with a long max-age and preload, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and a frame-ancestors CSP directive (or X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN for older browser support). Validate the final header set with a headers scanner after deployment.

References

  • OWASP Secure Headers Project
  • CWE-693 — Protection Mechanism Failure
  • MDN Web Docs — HTTP security headers

Name: Outdated or Vulnerable Software Component
Description:
# Description

A service or component reachable at {{AFFECTED}} is running an outdated version with known, published vulnerabilities, identified via banner/version fingerprinting and correlated against public CVE records.

# Impact

Exposure to publicly documented, often publicly-exploited vulnerabilities in the identified version — the specific impact (information disclosure through remote code execution) depends on which CVE applies, but the exploit path is already public and requires no discovery work from an attacker.

# Replication Steps
  • Version identified via service/banner fingerprinting; correlate the reported version against the vendor's advisories and the NVD for applicable CVEs.
Recommendation:
Patch or upgrade the affected component to a supported, fixed release — check the specific CVE(s) identified for the exact fixed version, since a minor bump is not always sufficient. Establish a recurring patch-management cadence rather than a one-time fix, and remove unused or end-of-life software entirely rather than leaving it reachable.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A06:2021 — Vulnerable and Outdated Components
  • CWE-1104 — Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components
  • NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD)

Name: Exposed Administrative or Debug Endpoint
Description:
# Description

An administrative, management, or debug interface is reachable at {{TARGET_URL}} without adequate authentication or network-level restriction — it should require a login (or should not be internet-reachable at all) and does neither.

# Impact

Depending on the interface, unauthenticated reach can yield configuration changes, credential access, or remote code execution (many admin/debug consoles expose an eval-style console or file upload by design) — a direct path to full compromise of the application or its host, not merely information exposure.

# Replication Steps
  • Access the identified endpoint(s) directly and confirm no authentication is enforced: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Require strong authentication plus MFA on every management interface, and restrict network reach to a trusted range or VPN rather than relying on authentication alone as the only control. Remove debug endpoints and consoles from production builds entirely — gate them behind a build flag that cannot be enabled by an environment variable an attacker could influence.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A05:2021 — Security Misconfiguration
  • CWE-749 — Exposed Dangerous Method or Function

Name: Weak TLS/SSL Configuration
Description:
# Description

The service at {{AFFECTED}} negotiates weak TLS protocol versions or cipher suites (SSLv3/TLS 1.0/1.1, RC4, export- or NULL-strength ciphers), presents an expired, self-signed, or hostname-mismatched certificate, or is otherwise vulnerable to a known TLS downgrade/attack class.

# Impact

Weakened confidentiality and integrity of data in transit, enabling protocol downgrade or man-in-the-middle interception of sensitive data (session tokens, credentials, PII) by a network-positioned attacker — the severity scales with how sensitive the data crossing this connection is.

# Replication Steps
  • Enumerate supported protocols/ciphers and the certificate chain: sslscan {{TARGET_HOST}} or testssl.sh {{TARGET_HOST}}
Recommendation:
Disable SSLv3/TLS 1.0/1.1 entirely; enable only TLS 1.2+ with modern AEAD cipher suites (no RC4, no export/NULL ciphers); deploy a valid certificate from a trusted CA with the correct hostname(s); and enable HSTS once TLS is consistently correct. Follow the Mozilla TLS "Intermediate" configuration profile as a baseline and re-scan after the change to confirm the weak options are actually gone, not just deprioritized.

References

  • Mozilla Server Side TLS Guidelines
  • CWE-326 — Inadequate Encryption Strength
  • NIST SP 800-52r2 — TLS Guidelines

Name: Kubernetes Security Misconfiguration
Description:
# Description

Posture scanning of the Kubernetes cluster identified control failures against recognized frameworks (NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance, MITRE ATT&CK for Containers) — for example privileged or host-namespace workloads, missing default-deny NetworkPolicies, over-permissive RBAC bindings, or pods running without a restricted security context (root user, writable root filesystem, unneeded Linux capabilities retained).

# Impact

Weakened workload isolation and blast-radius controls. Failing controls are rarely exploited in isolation — a privileged pod plus over-permissive RBAC is a direct container-escape-to-cluster-admin chain, while a missing NetworkPolicy turns a single compromised pod into free lateral movement across the whole namespace or cluster.

# Replication Steps
  • Scan against the target kubeconfig: kubescape scan framework nsa,mitre --format json

Failing control(s): {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Remediate the failing control(s) above: enforce Pod Security Standards at restricted, apply least-privilege RBAC (no wildcard verbs/resources, no cluster-admin bindings beyond genuine operators), default-deny NetworkPolicies with explicit allow rules per workload, and non-root/read-only-root security contexts with capabilities dropped to the minimum a workload actually needs. Re-run the same scan after remediation to confirm each control now passes rather than assuming the config change took effect.

References

  • NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance
  • MITRE ATT&CK for Containers
  • CIS Kubernetes Benchmark

Name: Exposed Network Service
Description:
# Description

Service fingerprinting identified network service(s) exposed on {{AFFECTED}} that may be unnecessary, unauthenticated, or reachable from a broader network segment than the service's design intends — commonly databases, management/administration protocols, or legacy services that should be internal-only.

# Impact

Expands the attack surface reachable from the tested network position; unauthenticated or weakly-authenticated exposed services are consistently among the fastest initial-access and lateral-movement vectors because they require no phishing, no credential theft, and no prior foothold — only network reach.

# Replication Steps
  • Service(s) and banner(s) captured during fingerprinting: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Restrict each exposed service above to the minimum network segment that genuinely needs it (firewalling/segmentation), require authentication on anything that currently has none, disable or remove services with no active business use, and place management/administration protocols behind a bastion host or VPN rather than exposing them directly.

References

  • CIS Controls — Network Infrastructure Management
  • OWASP Top 10 A05:2021 — Security Misconfiguration
